newsitem.title: INDIA: Americans warned after Sikh extradited to India.
newsitem.headline: Americans warned after Sikh extradited to India.

text.p: The United States has warned its citizens living in India of possible retaliation by separatist insurgents following the extradition of a suspected Sikh militant leader, U.S. officials said on Wednesday.

A U.S. embassy notice advised Americans to "review their security posture and increase their awareness" following the extradition to India last week of Daya Singh Lahoria, accused by New Delhi of attempted assassination and kidnapping.
Lahoria, also known as Sandhu, was extradited to India last Thursday.
He is believed to be one of the leaders of the Khalistan Liberation Force, a militant group fighting for a separate Sikh nation in the northern state of Punjab.
"Although the Embassy is not in possession of any specific information regarding threats to American citizens, we cannot discount the possibility of acts of anti-American violence," the notice said.
"It should be noted that Sikh terrorists are still capable of performing violent acts," it said.

Thousands of people died in insurgency-related violence during a decade-long Sikh rebellion against New Delhi's rule in Punjab state, India's bread basket which was split between India and Pakistan during partition in 1947.
The revolt peaked in 1984 when soldiers stormed the Golden Temple in Amritsar, considered the holiest Sikh shrine. Later that year, prime minister Indira Gandhi was killed by her Sikh bodyguards.
The insurgency subsided in the early 1990s, and local elections were held in 1992 amid a security clampdown.
New elections are due on February 7, and thousands of paramilitary troops are set to fan out across the state.
Earlier this month a U.S. court cleared the way for the extradition of Lahoria, who was arrested in 1995.

The Central Bureau of Investigation, India's federal police agency, said Lahoria was wanted for the attempted assassination in September 1993 of the then head of the Congress party's youth wing, M.S. Bitta. Nine people were killed and 23 injured in the bombing of the Indian Youth Congress building in Delhi.
Lahoria was also suspected of involvement in the abduction of the son of former government minister Ram Niwas Mirdha, as well as arms trafficking in India, authorities said.

India praised the United States last week for extraditing Lahoria, saying the move would send a signal that the two countries, which are considering an extradition treaty, were cooperating to combat militancy.
After being extradited, Lahoria was remanded to custody in the western state of Rajasthan, not Punjab where his supporters had feared he might receive harsher treatment.
Diplomats said India had assured Washington that Lahoria would be able to meet regularly in prison with representatives of an international aid organisation to ensure he was in good health.
